title: Foundation Models Are Probabilistic, Not Deterministic
why: Trains you to treat a model output as a sampled distribution to be tested, not a return value to be trusted.
explanation: When you call a model, it doesn't "know" the answer and hand it back. At each step it computes a probability over the next token and samples one. That sampling is why the same prompt can give you a clean JSON object one call and a chatty pa

title: Prompting as Engineering, Not Vibes
why: Trains the judgment to treat a prompt as a versioned, testable spec (system vs user, zero/few-shot, structured output) instead of trial-and-error text.
explanation: A prompt is not a chat message you tweak until it looks right. It's a specification for behavior, and it deserves the same discipline as any other spec: it lives in version control, it has a name and a version, and it's tied to a test set.

title: The Augmented LLM: Tools and Function Calling
why: Trains you to design tool definitions with docstring-quality clarity and examples so the model can actually invoke them correctly.
explanation: A tool definition is an API contract written for a reader who never sees your code and can't ask follow-up questions. The model decides whether and how to call your function based entirely on the name, the description, and the parameter doc

title: LLM-as-Judge, Validated First
why: Trains the judgment of when a model grader is trustworthy: use rubrics, make it reason-then-score, use a different model, and prove it against human labels before scaling.

why: Trains the hardest Principal call: deciding where AI does — and does not — belong across the org, and driving that direction through influence rather than authority.
